sub_answers.text: Deformation theory can be controlled by pre-Lie algebra structures, with a new integration theory for pre-Lie algebras providing explicit formulae and gauge elements that govern transfers of homotopy algebra structures [d26245s0p0]. Hom-pre-Lie bialgebras are developed within a cohomological framework which allows the study of coboundary Hom-pre-Lie bialgebras and provides constructions via Hom-s-matrices [d55626s0p0]. Hom-O-operators and Hom-L-dendriform structures are used to construct Hom-s-matrices and thus produce explicit Hom-pre-Lie bialgebra deformations [d55626s0p0].

sub_answers.text: Hom-type algebras can be produced from classical algebras by twisting with self-morphisms, i.e., the category of Hom-Lie-Yamaguti algebras is closed under twisting by self-morphisms [d9858s0p0]. Constructions of Hom-type algebras are given from classical Lie-Yamaguti algebras and from Malcev algebras, illustrating that standard Hom-algebras arise via such twisting procedures from their classical counterparts [d9858s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Relationship between pre-Lie algebras and their associated Lie algebras via commutator bracket
Formulation of the Hom-Jacobi identity and how it modifies the classical Jacobi identity
Expression of pre-Lie identity and its Hom-version under a twisting endomorphism
Definition of derivations of Hom-algebras and how twisting affects the Leibniz rule
Construction of universal enveloping algebras for Hom-Lie algebras and corresponding PBW-type statements
Cohomology theories for Hom-Lie or Hom-pre-Lie algebras and the role of the twisting map in differentials

What obstructions (cohomology classes, compatibility conditions, or explicit counterexamples) prevent the existence of nonzero derivations D on a Hom-algebra (A, μ, α) that satisfy D∘α = α∘D and the Hom-Leibniz rule; list known obstruction groups, spectral-sequence criteria, or explicit Hom-algebra families where any α-preserving derivation must be inner or trivial

Survey specific examples and published results where classical Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt type theorems or universal enveloping algebra constructions fail in Hom-Lie or Hom-associative settings: describe the failure modes (graded dimensions, relations, filtered-graded isomorphism breakdown), known families of Hom-algebras lacking PBW bases, and counterexamples to naive enveloping algebra functors

In what ways do standard Hochschild, Chevalley–Eilenberg, or derived-functor cohomology theories fail to classify or detect infinitesimal deformations, extension classes, or obstructions for Hom-associative and Hom-Lie algebras; cite specific missing cohomology operations, examples where usual deformation-obstruction correspondence breaks, or modified cohomology proposals that address these gaps

What obstacles arise when attempting to define or classify fiberwise Hom-algebra structures on vector bundles, principal bundles, or sheaves (for example, compatibility of the twisting map with transition functions, existence of local α-trivializations, stacky obstructions, or Cech cohomology obstructions); provide concrete examples where global Hom-structures cannot be glued from local data

List open problems, conjectures, and precise unanswered questions about rigidity, integrability, deformation classification, and moduli of affine-twisted Hom-algebras (e.g., criteria for formal rigidity, existence of versal deformations, classification of low-dimensional examples, and whether certain integrability/quantization procedures extend to affine-twisted Hom-structures)

Give precise definitions of modules and representation categories for Hom-Lie algebras (including Hom-modules, morphisms, and module axioms with structure map compatibility), describe common classes of representations (simple, indecomposable, highest-weight-like, weight-space decompositions) and give explicit examples comparing these to classical Lie algebra representations to highlight which properties change and why.

Characterize the derivation algebra of a Hom-type algebra: define inner versus outer derivations in the Hom-context, give criteria and cohomological conditions distinguishing them, compute Der(H) for key examples (e.g., finite-dimensional Hom-Lie algebras coming from Yau twists of sl2 or Heisenberg), and explain how central extensions and the Hom-structure map affect the space of outer derivations.

Explain the role of Hom-pre-Lie and Hom-Gerstenhaber structures in formal deformation theory: derive explicit deformation formulas (Maurer–Cartan equations, cup/bracket operations, and first-order deformation cocycles) for Hom-associative/Hom-Lie algebras, give worked examples of one-parameter families using Hom-pre-Lie algebra data, and show how classical deformation techniques are modified by the twisting map.

Describe geometric applications of Hom-algebra structures: define Hom-connections and Hom-affine structures, state curvature and torsion formulas adapted to the Hom-setting, and give criteria for flatness of Hom-connections; provide examples linking Hom-Lie algebroids or Hom-Lie groupoids to affine manifolds, local geometric models, or fiber bundle constructions where the Hom-structure is geometric.

Provide explicit examples from mathematical physics where twisting (e.g., Yau twist or q-twists) produces genuinely new Lie-type actions or modified symmetry algebras: list models (quantum deformations, q-Poincaré, deformed gauge algebras, integrable systems, sigma-model symmetry algebras), compute the altered commutators/structure constants and conserved charges in one or two concrete cases, and explain how these twisted symmetries change representation content or physical observables.

Precise definition of a Hom-Lie algebra: list the structure (vector space, bilinear bracket, linear twisting map), state the skew-symmetry requirement, and write the Hom-Jacobi identity explicitly in terms of the twisting map; include variations (multiplicative Hom-Lie, regular Hom-Lie) and minimal axioms used in the literature.

Formal definition of a pre-Lie algebra (also called a left-symmetric algebra): give the bilinear product and the left-symmetry (associator) identity, show how the antisymmetrized product yields a Lie bracket, and cite the standard equivalence statements connecting pre-Lie algebras to Lie-admissible algebras.

Clarify what is meant by an affine twist or an affine action in algebra: define an affine action of an algebraic structure on a vector space (semidirect product / affine representation), describe the construction that twists a product by an affine map (translation plus linear part), and provide the formal conditions under which this yields a new algebraic structure.

Concrete standard examples of Hom-type algebras obtained by Yau twist: give the Yau twisting procedure (starting from an associative algebra or Lie algebra and an algebra endomorphism), write the new twisted product or bracket formula, and list canonical examples from the literature (e.g., Hom-associative from associative, Hom-Lie from Lie, examples using matrix algebras and polynomial algebras).

Explicit description of the relationship between a pre-Lie algebra and its associated Lie algebra: prove that the commutator [x,y]=x·y−y·x satisfies the Lie axioms, show how the left-symmetry identity implies the Jacobi identity for the commutator, and note consequences for representations and enveloping algebras.

Give the precise formula of the Hom-Jacobi identity for a Hom-Lie algebra (specify the bracket [ , ] and twisting map α) and explain concretely how each term differs from the classical Jacobi identity for Lie algebras; include an example computation showing the α-twist acting on one cyclic permutation.

Write the standard pre-Lie (left-symmetric) identity in tensor or component form, then derive the Hom-pre-Lie identity obtained when inserting a linear twisting map β; state the exact positions where β is applied and present an explicit example comparing the two identities on basis elements.

Provide a formal definition of a derivation D of a Hom-algebra (give both degree-0 and degree-k versions if relevant), state the modified Leibniz rule involving the twisting map (α∘D versus D∘α, etc.), and give a concrete example of a linear map that is a derivation in the Hom-setting but not in the ordinary algebra setting.

Describe constructions proposed in the literature for universal enveloping algebras of a Hom-Lie algebra (e.g., quotient of tensor algebra with twisted relations, Hom-associative enveloping constructions), state any known Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt-type theorems or counterexamples, and specify the extra hypotheses (like multiplicativity or regularity of the twist) required for PBW statements.

List cohomology complexes defined for Hom-Lie and Hom-pre-Lie algebras (specify cochain spaces, differential operators dα), show how the twisting map α enters the differential formula and coboundary condition, and indicate how cocycles and coboundaries differ from the classical Chevalley–Eilenberg case with a short example of a 2-cocycle condition.

What specific obstructions, cohomology classes, or structural conditions prevent the existence of nonzero derivations D that commute with or preserve a given Hom-twist α (i.e., D ∘ α = α ∘ D) in concrete families such as Hom-Lie, Hom-associative, and α-derivation modules; are there results describing centroid, centralizer or fixed-point subalgebra criteria that force only trivial α-derivations?

Where and why do PBW-type theorems and universal enveloping algebra constructions fail in the Hom-setting: provide explicit counterexamples or classification results (e.g., graded dimension mismatches, relations that obstruct a PBW basis) for Hom-Lie → Hom-associative enveloping maps, and references to counterexamples or negative results by authors working on Hom-PBW analogues

Which versions of cohomology (Hom-Hochschild, Hom-Chevalley–Eilenberg, cyclic or Harrison-type theories) are known to be insufficient to detect or classify small deformations and nontrivial extensions of Hom-algebras; identify specific low-degree failure modes (vanishing H^2, undetected obstruction classes in H^3) and examples where standard cohomology misses nontrivial formal deformations

What obstacles arise when trying to define, glue, or classify fiberwise Hom-structures (e.g., Hom-vector bundles, Hom-algebra bundles, Hom-sheaves) over topological spaces or schemes: precise problems with local triviality, transition maps twisted by α, Čech obstruction classes, existence of principal Hom-bundles or Hom-gerbes, and explicit examples where a fiberwise Hom-structure cannot be globally defined

What are the main open questions and conjectures about rigidity, formal integrability, and classification for affine-twisted Hom-algebras (affine Hom-Lie/associative types), including conjectured necessary/sufficient invariants, expected moduli descriptions, and known partial results or barriers to proving rigidity or integrability in families?

List and explain the definitions of modules, representations, and module homomorphisms for Hom-Lie algebras; compare these with classical Lie algebra representations and specify exactly which axioms are modified, with citations to papers that introduce alternative representation categories (e.g., Yau-twists, adjoint vs. coadjoint modules).

Describe criteria and structure theorems that determine the derivation algebra of a Hom-type algebra: how to identify inner derivations, construct outer derivations, compute the first cohomology H^1 for Hom-Lie and Hom-associative examples, and list worked computations for specific finite-dimensional Hom-Lie algebras.

Provide explicit formulations of Hom-pre-Lie (Hom-left-symmetric) algebra deformations: give the deformation complex, Maurer–Cartan-type equations, low-order deformation formulas, and sample computations showing how Hom-pre-Lie structures control associative/Lie-type deformations.

Survey geometric interpretations of Hom-algebra structures: examples where Hom-Lie or Hom-associative brackets arise from (twisted) connections, affine manifolds, flat torsion-free connections, or fiber bundle constructions; include precise constructions mapping geometric data (connection, holonomy, monodromy) to Hom-algebra operations.

Give concrete examples from mathematical physics where applying a twisting map (σ, α, etc.) to a Lie algebra yields new symmetry algebras or modified Lie actions: include deformed current algebras, q-deformations, sigma-model symmetry twists, explicit commutation relations before and after twisting, and references to models where these alter conserved charges or equations of motion.

Precise definition of a Hom-Lie algebra: list the structure (vector space, bilinear bracket, linear self-map), state axioms including skew-symmetry of the bracket, the Hom-Jacobi identity written explicitly (α([x,y]) = ? or [α(x),[y,z]] + cyclic = 0 form), and clarify the role and properties required of the twisting map (multiplicativity, invertibility conditions, examples of weak vs. multiplicative Hom-Lie).

Formal definition of a pre-Lie algebra (also called left-symmetric algebra): give the bilinear product identity (left-symmetry: (x·y)·z - x·(y·z) = (y·x)·z - y·(x·z)), list axioms over a field, and explain the construction that produces a Lie algebra via the commutator [x,y] = x·y - y·x; cite relations to affine manifolds, Courant algebroids, and examples like endomorphism algebras and rooted tree pre-Lie structures.

Explicit definition and construction of an affine twist/affine action in algebraic contexts: describe an affine action of a Lie or associative algebra on a vector space (linear part plus translation), define an affine twist map (combining an algebra endomorphism with a translation or 1-cocycle), and give formulas for how the twist modifies products or brackets (e.g., new product x ⋆ y = φ(x)·ψ(y)+τ(x,y)), with references to semidirect products and cocycle deformation language.

Catalogue of standard examples of Hom-algebras produced by the Yau twist: give the Yau twist procedure (starting from associative or Lie algebra and an algebra endomorphism α, define new product [x,y]_α = α([x,y]) or x⋆y = α(x·y)), and list concrete examples—Hom-associative and Hom-Lie algebras obtained from matrix algebras, polynomial algebras with scaling maps, the Witt and Virasoro algebras with q-deformations—showing the form of the twisted identities.

Detailed description of the relationship between a pre-Lie algebra and its associated Lie algebra: prove or state that the commutator bracket [x,y] = x·y - y·x satisfies the Lie axioms, explain how the left multiplication operators L_x give a representation of that Lie algebra, and discuss conditions under which the pre-Lie structure splits (modules, cohomology viewpoint) and examples illustrating the passage from pre-Lie to Lie.

Give the precise formula of the Hom-Jacobi identity for a Hom-Lie algebra (V, [·,·], α). Explain explicitly how each term differs from the classical Jacobi identity and describe conditions on α where the Hom-Jacobi reduces to the ordinary Jacobi identity.

Write the standard pre-Lie (right-symmetric) identity in tensor/index form and then state the Hom-pre-Lie identity for a bilinear product · and a twisting map α. Show how α is inserted into each associator term and give examples of α where the Hom-version collapses to the usual pre-Lie relation.

Define what it means for a linear map D on a Hom-algebra (A, μ, α) to be a derivation. Present the modified Leibniz rule involving α (or its powers), list variants (α-derivation, α^k-derivation), and state necessary compatibility conditions between D and α.

Describe constructions in the literature of universal enveloping algebras for Hom-Lie algebras: the underlying free Hom-associative algebra, quotient by Hom-ideal generated by relations, and explicit PBW-type bases or graded isomorphism statements. Indicate hypotheses (nilpotency, multiplicativity, α invertible) used to prove PBW theorems.

Enumerate cohomology complexes defined for Hom-Lie and Hom-pre-Lie algebras: cochain spaces, coboundary maps, and how the twisting map α enters the differential (pre- and post-composition, weight factors). Compare known cohomology theories (Yau cohomology, Hom-Lie cohomology) and describe how α affects low-dimensional cohomology groups and deformation theory.
